_comment: FIXTURE CORPUS - NOT THE REAL KNOWLEDGE BASE.
Sixteen short passages standing in for pages on the domains CONNECT Plus
treats as trusted. The wording here is paraphrased guidance written for
this fixture, not text copied from those sites, and the URLs are
illustrative rather than live. Nothing was scraped, so no copyright or
crawling question attaches to this file.
Purpose: let stages 07-09 and the eval harness run before the RAG team
has crawled anything. Replace with real retrieval; do not extend this
file to look like a knowledge base.
Coverage is DELIBERATELY INCOMPLETE. There is nothing here about medical
advice, visas or immigration, or which phone to buy, because both eval
sets ask those questions and the correct behaviour is to refuse them.

The last entry is a POISONED chunk, used by the injection tests. It is

chunks.title: Recognising a scam text message
chunks.text: A scam text message often creates a sense of urgency, asks you to click a link, or claims there is a problem with an account. Genuine organisations do not ask you to confirm personal details through a link in a text message. If you are unsure, do not click the link. Contact the organisation using a phone number you already have, not one supplied in the message.

chunks.title: Prize and lottery scams
chunks.text: A message saying you have won a prize, a lottery or a gift card is almost always a scam, especially if you did not enter a competition. A genuine prize never requires you to pay a fee, a tax or a delivery charge before you receive it. If you are asked to send money to collect a prize, stop and do not send anything.

chunks.title: Report a scam
chunks.text: You can report a scam to Scamwatch online. Reporting helps warn other people even when your own money cannot be recovered. If you have lost money, contact your bank immediately and ask them to stop the transaction. If someone has your personal details, you can also contact IDCARE for free support.

chunks.title: Phone calls that pretend to be from a government agency
chunks.text: Scammers sometimes phone and claim to be from a government agency or the police, saying you owe money or your account is under investigation. A real government agency will never demand immediate payment by gift card, bank transfer or cryptocurrency, and will never threaten arrest over the phone. Hang up and call the agency back on a number from its official website.

chunks.title: Setting up two-factor authentication
chunks.text: Two-factor authentication adds a second check when you sign in. After you enter your password, a short verification code is sent to your phone, and you type that code to finish signing in. This means someone who learns your password still cannot get into your account. You can turn it on in your account security settings.

chunks.title: If someone asks you for your verification code
chunks.text: A verification code is for you alone. No genuine staff member from a bank, a government agency or a phone company will ever ask you to read your code out to them. If someone asks for your code by phone, text or email, it is a scam. End the contact and do not share the code.

chunks.title: Resetting a forgotten myGov password
chunks.text: If you have forgotten your myGov password you can reset it from the sign-in page by selecting the forgotten password option. You will be asked for your username or email address, and then for your secret questions or a code sent to your phone. If you cannot complete the reset, myGov has a phone help line that can verify your identity another way.

chunks.title: Signing in to myGov safely
chunks.text: Always reach myGov by typing the address into your browser yourself, rather than following a link in an email or text message. myGov will never send you a message asking you to sign in to fix a problem with your payment. If you receive a message like that, delete it and sign in the usual way to check your account.

chunks.title: Making text on your phone easier to read
chunks.text: You can make the writing on your phone bigger in the accessibility or display section of your settings. Look for a text size or font size slider and move it until the writing is comfortable to read. The change applies across most apps, so you only have to do it once.

chunks.title: Making a video call to family
chunks.text: A video call lets you see and hear the person you are speaking to. Open the app you use for messages, find the person's name in your contacts, and look for a camera symbol to start the call. If the other person cannot see you, check that the app has permission to use your camera in your phone settings.

chunks.title: Free training in using digital devices
chunks.text: Be Connected offers free online lessons and in-person sessions for older Australians learning to use phones, tablets and computers. Sessions are run at libraries and community centres across the country, and many venues can arrange help in languages other than English. You can search for a nearby location on the Be Connected website.

chunks.title: Checking whether a message is genuine
chunks.text: Before acting on a message, check the sender's address carefully, because a scam address often looks almost right with one letter changed. Be cautious about attachments and shortened links. If a message claims to come from an organisation you deal with, contact that organisation directly using details you already have to confirm whether the message is real.

chunks.title: Blocking unwanted calls and messages
chunks.text: You can block a number on your phone so it cannot call or message you again. Open the recent calls list, select the number, and choose the block option. Your phone company may also offer a call-blocking service. Blocking a number does not stop every scam call, because scammers change numbers often.

chunks.title: Mobile data and wifi
chunks.text: Wifi connects your device to the internet through a home or public network and does not use your mobile plan's data allowance. Mobile data uses your phone plan and counts towards your monthly limit. Connecting to wifi at home for large downloads and video calls helps you avoid extra charges.

chunks.title: Free interpreting services
chunks.text: TIS National provides interpreting services for people who do not speak English fluently, and the service is free when you are contacting many government agencies. You can phone the service and ask for an interpreter in your language, and the interpreter will join the call with the agency. Many community health services can also book an interpreter for your appointment.

chunks.title: Getting help with Centrelink by phone
chunks.text: Services Australia has separate phone lines for different payments and services, and a multilingual phone line for people who prefer to speak in a language other than English. Call waiting times are usually shorter early in the morning. Have your customer reference number ready before you call so staff can find your record quickly.
